![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226336/assets/85730909004322c2c8b6d065ff1cdb4b0662830007bd5aa14c8c8c4bda798206.png)

The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$ (shown above) is given by the integral

$$
A=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?
question.worked_solution:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $3$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226336/assets/85730909004322c2c8b6d065ff1cdb4b0662830007bd5aa14c8c8c4bda798206.png)

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=0$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{3}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{3}=0+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{3}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $3$ petals of our rose:

$$
{{[0,\frac{\pi }{3}]}_{⏟}}_{1\text{st}},\,{{[\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{2\pi }{3}]}_{⏟}}_{2\text{nd}},\,{{[\frac{2\pi }{3},\pi ]}_{⏟}}_{3\text{rd}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =0$ to $\theta =\pi :$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$
